claim: The unfolded protein response (UPR) maintains protein folding homeostasis in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: The unfolded protein response (UPR) maintains protein folding homeostasis in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is a well-established concept in cell biology supported by extensive literature.

claim: In metazoan cells, the Ire1 branch of the UPR initiates two functional outputs—non-conventional mRNA splicing and selective mRNA decay (RIDD).
source: In metazoan cells, the Ire1 branch of the UPR initiates two functional outputs—non-conventional mRNA splicing and selective mRNA decay (RIDD).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is referenced in the introduction.

claim: Ire1 orthologs from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe are specialized for only splicing or RIDD, respectively.
source: By contrast, Ire1 orthologs from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe are specialized for only splicing or RIDD, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the manuscript and experimental data presented.

claim: The functional specialization of Ire1 lies in Ire1's RNase activity, which is either stringently splice-site specific or promiscuous.
source: Previously, we showed that the functional specialization lies in Ire1's RNase activity, which is either stringently splice-site specific or promiscuous (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Conversion of two amino acids within the RNase domain of S. cerevisiae Ire1 to their S. pombe counterparts rendered it promiscuous.
source: We found that conversion of two amino acids within the RNase domain of S. cerevisiae Ire1 to their S. pombe counterparts rendered it promiscuous.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mutations rewired a pair of salt bridges at Ire1 RNase domain's dimer interface, changing its protomer alignment.
source: Using biochemical assays and computational modeling, we show that the mutations rewired a pair of salt bridges at Ire1 RNase domain's dimer interface, changing its protomer alignment.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays and computational modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ire1 protomer alignment affects its substrates specificity.
source: Thus, Ire1 protomer alignment affects its substrates specificity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data and modeling.

claim: About one third of all proteins in eukaryotes are folded in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: In eukaryotes, about one third of all proteins are folded in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: The most evolutionarily conserved branch of the UPR is initiated by Ire1, an ER-transmembrane kinase/endoribonuclease (RNase).
source: The most evolutionarily conserved branch of the UPR is initiated by Ire1, an ER-transmembrane kinase/endoribonuclease (RNase).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: In response to accumulated unfolded proteins in the ER, Ire1 forms oligomers.
source: In response to accumulated unfolded proteins in the ER, Ire1 forms oligomers (Aragón et al., 2009; Korennykh et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010) and carries out two functional outputs.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Ire1 initiates non-conventional splicing of HAC1 (in S. cerevisiae) or XBP1 (in metazoans) mRNA.
source: First, Ire1 initiates non-conventional splicing of HAC1 (in S. cerevisiae) or XBP1 (in metazoans) mRNA (Cox et al., 1993; Mori et al., 1993; Sidrauski and Walter, 1997; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: After cleavage by Ire1 and removal of the intron, the severed exons are ligated by tRNA ligase.
source: After cleavage by Ire1 and removal of the intron, the severed exons are ligated by tRNA ligase (Jurkin et al., 2014; Kosmaczewski et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Peschek et al., 2015; Peschek and Walter, 2019; Sidrauski et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The spliced mRNAs are translated into Hac1 and Xbp1 proteins, both of which are transcription factors that induce the UPR gene expression program in the nucleus.
source: The spliced mRNAs are translated into Hac1 and Xbp1 proteins, both of which are transcription factors that induce the UPR gene expression program in the nucleus (Calfon et al., 2002; Travers et al., 2000; Van Dalfsen et al., 2018; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Ire1 selectively cleaves a set of mRNAs that encode ER-targeted proteins.
source: Second, Ire1 selectively cleaves a set of mRNAs that encode ER-targeted proteins.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: The cleaved mRNAs are subsequently degraded by the cellular RNA decay machinery.
source: The cleaved mRNAs are subsequently degraded by the cellular RNA decay machinery (Guydosh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Regulated Ire1-dependent mRNA decay (RIDD) restores homeostasis of the ER by reducing the protein folding burden.
source: As a result, this process, known as regulated Ire1-dependent mRNA decay (RIDD), restores homeostasis of the ER by reducing the protein folding burden (Bae et al., 2019; Hollien et al., 2009; Hollien and Weissman, 2006; Kimmig et al., 2012; Moore and Hollien, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: S. cerevisiae Ire1 initiates splicing of HAC1 mRNA as its singular target in the cell.
source: S. cerevisiae Ire1 initiates splicing of HAC1 mRNA as its singular target in the cell (Niwa et al., 2005), and S. pombe Ire1 exclusively performs RIDD (Guydosh et al., 2017; Kimmig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: S. pombe Ire1 exclusively performs RIDD.
source: S. cerevisiae Ire1 initiates splicing of HAC1 mRNA as its singular target in the cell (Niwa et al., 2005), and S. pombe Ire1 exclusively performs RIDD (Guydosh et al., 2017; Kimmig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: S. cerevisiae Ire1 has a stringent RNase, restricting it to HAC1 mRNA.
source: S. cerevisiae Ire1 has a stringent RNase, restricting it to HAC1 mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: S. pombe Ire1 has a promiscuous (i.e. broadly specific) RNase, enabling cleavage of a wide range of mRNA RIDD targets.
source: In contrast, S. pombe Ire1 has a promiscuous (i.e. broadly specific) RNase, enabling cleavage of a wide range of mRNA RIDD targets.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: E. coli cells bearing a plasmid containing the Sp IRE1-KR barely grew within the monitored 5 hr time window, even in the absence of the IPTG inducer.
source: Growth curves revealed that E. coli cells bearing a plasmid containing the Sp IRE1-KR barely grew within the monitored 5 hr time window, even in the absence of the isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) inducer (Figure 1A, blue filled triangles).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: E. coli cells bearing plasmids containing Sc IRE1-KR grew normally with a growth rate comparable to that of a control strain bearing an empty plasmid.
source: By contrast, E. coli cells bearing plasmids containing Sc IRE1-KR grew normally with a growth rate comparable to that of a control strain bearing an empty plasmid.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The T7 promoter is known to exhibit background expression even in the absence of IPTG.
source: Because the T7 promoter is known to exhibit background expression even in the absence of IPTG (Rosano and Ceccarelli, 2014), we reasoned that the observed gene toxicity of Sp IRE1-KR might result from the enzyme's promiscuous RNase activity, which may degrade endogenous E. coli RNAs required for viability.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The observed gene toxicity of Sp IRE1-KR might result from the enzyme's promiscuous RNase activity, which may degrade endogenous E. coli RNAs required for viability.
source: Because the T7 promoter is known to exhibit background expression even in the absence of IPTG (Rosano and Ceccarelli, 2014), we reasoned that the observed gene toxicity of Sp IRE1-KR might result from the enzyme's promiscuous RNase activity, which may degrade endogenous E. coli RNAs required for viability.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR might be tolerated because of its exquisite substrate specificity for Sc HAC1 mRNA splice junctions.
source: By contrast, Sc Ire1-KR might be tolerated, because of its exquisite substrate specificity for Sc HAC1 mRNA splice junctions (Niwa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference and supported by citation.

claim: 4µ8C inhibited cleavage of a 21 base-pair stem-loop substrate derived from the 3' splice junction of XBP1 mRNA for both Sp and Sc Ire1-KR.
source: As expected, 4µ8C inhibited cleavage of a 21 base-pair stem-loop substrate derived from the 3' splice junction of XBP1 mRNA for both Sp and Sc Ire1-KR (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), as well as RIDD activity in Sp cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B, 1C, and supplementary figures.

claim: 4µ8C inhibited RIDD activity in Sp cells.
source: As expected, 4µ8C inhibited cleavage of a 21 base-pair stem-loop substrate derived from the 3' splice junction of XBP1 mRNA for both Sp and Sc Ire1-KR (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), as well as RIDD activity in Sp cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: When added to the cultures of cells bearing plasmids encoding Sp Ire1-KR, 4µ8C restored normal growth.
source: Importantly, when added to the cultures of cells bearing plasmids encoding Sp Ire1-KR, 4µ8C restored normal growth (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An RNase-dead mutant of Sp Ire1-KR harboring the H1018A mutation was not toxic.
source: In further agreement with the notion that Sp RNase activity was the culprit of reduced E. coli growth, an RNase-dead mutant of Sp Ire1-KR harboring the H1018A mutation (Kimmig et al., 2012) was not toxic (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citation to previous work.

claim: E. coli growth was inhibited by the endonuclease activity, rather than by indirect effects, such as protein misfolding or aggregation.
source: These results suggest that E. coli growth was inhibited by the endonuclease activity, rather than by indirect effects, such as protein misfolding or aggregation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results with 4µ8C and the RNase-dead mutant.

claim: Bacterial growth can be exploited to assess substrate specificity of Ire1's RNase.
source: Moreover, we established that bacterial growth can be exploited to assess substrate specificity of Ire1's RNase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Seventeen residues were selected as candidate residues that may regulate Ire1's RNase promiscuity based on their location and divergence between Sc and Sp.
source: Using structure-guided sequence comparison of Ire1 RNase domains, we picked a total of seventeen residues whose common features include that they are (i) part of an oligomerization interface or located within 18 Å from the helix-loop element (HLE), which contains a positively charged loop (N1036 to K1042 on Sc Ire1) that engages the RNA substrates (Korennykh et al., 2009; Korennykh et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2008), and (ii) divergent amino acids between Sc and Sp but conserved within the Schizosaccharomyces genus.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and sequence comparison, supported by citations.

claim: Among the seventeen amino acids, seven are located near the HLE, five are located at the RNase-RNase interface within the back-to-back dimer, and five are located at the RNase-RNase interface in the active Ire1 oligomer.
source: Among the seventeen amino acids, seven are located near the HLE, five are located at the RNase-RNase interface within the back-to-back dimer (previously defined as interface IF1C Korennykh et al., 2009), and five are located at the RNase-RNase interface in the active Ire1 oligomer (previously defined as interface IF2C Korennykh et al., 2009; Figure 2A & B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2A & B.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR-mut17 efficiently and specifically cleaved all four stem-loop RNA substrates with comparable kinetics.
source: Remarkably, Sc Ire1-KR-mut17 efficiently and specifically cleaved all four stem-loop RNA substrates (Figure 2C–F) with comparable kinetics (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C-G.

claim: Introducing the 17 mutations made Sc Ire1 more 'pombe-like' regarding its acceptance of variable-loop RIDD substrates.
source: These results show that introducing the 17 mutations made Sc Ire1 more 'pombe-like' regarding its acceptance of variable-loop RIDD substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The expression of Ire1-KR-mut17 proved toxic and 4µ8C alleviated the toxicity.
source: When tested in the E. coli growth assay, the expression of Ire1-KR-mut17 proved toxic and 4µ8C alleviated the toxicity (Figure 2H), confirming the notion that toxicity results from the enzyme's broadened substrate range.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Toxicity results from the enzyme's broadened substrate range.
source: When tested in the E. coli growth assay, the expression of Ire1-KR-mut17 proved toxic and 4µ8C alleviated the toxicity (Figure 2H), confirming the notion that toxicity results from the enzyme's broadened substrate range.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Three revertants (K992, H1044, and Y1059) showed markedly reduced toxicity.
source: We found that three revertants (K992, H1044, and Y1059) showed markedly reduced toxicity, whereas the other 14 revertants remained toxic (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,H1044D,Y1059R) cleaved both Sp stem-loop and Sc HAC1 3' splice-site substrates efficiently and with similar rates.
source: Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,H1044D,Y1059R) cleaved both Sp stem-loop and Sc HAC1 3' splice-site substrates efficiently (Figure 3B–E) and with similar rates (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B-F.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) cleaved both Sc and Sp stem-loop RNA substrates with efficiencies comparable to those of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,H1044D,Y1059R).
source: Recombinantly expressed and purified Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) cleaved both Sc and Sp stem-loop RNA substrates with efficiencies comparable to those of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,H1044D,Y1059R) (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B-F.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(H1044D) cleaved the cognate Sc RNA substrate but none of the Sp RNA substrates.
source: By contrast, Sc Ire1-KR(H1044D) cleaved the cognate Sc RNA substrate but none of the Sp RNA substrates (Figure 3B–F), suggesting that the two cerevisiae-to-pombe mutations at Ire1's RNase-RNase dimer interface confer Ire1 RNase promiscuity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B-F.

claim: The two cerevisiae-to-pombe mutations at Ire1's RNase-RNase dimer interface confer Ire1 RNase promiscuity.
source: By contrast, Sc Ire1-KR(H1044D) cleaved the cognate Sc RNA substrate but none of the Sp RNA substrates (Figure 3B–F), suggesting that the two cerevisiae-to-pombe mutations at Ire1's RNase-RNase dimer interface confer Ire1 RNase promiscuity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: H1044D appears a false positive, likely isolated because the bacterial assay cannot distinguish stringent RNase from inactive RNase as neither is toxic to the bacterial cells.
source: By contrast, H1044D appears a false positive, likely isolated because the bacterial assay cannot distinguish stringent RNase from inactive RNase as neither is toxic to the bacterial cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: WT Sc Ire1-KR showed specificity for the sequence motif CNG|(C/A)NGN.
source: Using the HAC1-derived mutant substrates, we showed that WT Sc Ire1-KR showed specificity for the sequence motif CNG|(C/A)NGN, in close agreement with previous findings (Gonzalez et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) recognized a less-stringent sequence motif, CNG|NNGN, in particular tolerating base substitutions in the +1 position.
source: By comparison, Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) recognized a less-stringent sequence motif, CNG|NNGN, in particular tolerating base substitutions in the +1 position (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The 9-membered stem loops were not cleaved by WT Sc Ire1-KR.
source: The 9-membered stem loops were not cleaved by WT Sc Ire1-KR, in line with previous study (Gonzalez et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: The 9-membered stem loops were cleaved by Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R).
source: By contrast, the same RNAs were cleaved by Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The two interface mutations in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) render the enzyme more tolerant to both RNA sequence and loop size variations.
source: The results suggest that the two interface mutations in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) render the enzyme more tolerant to both RNA sequence and loop size variations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A stem-loop RNA substrate containing the Sp BIP1 cleavage site was efficiently cleaved by Sp Ire1-KR but not by Sc Ire1-KR.
source: We confirmed that a stem-loop RNA substrate containing this site was efficiently cleaved by Sp Ire1-KR but not by Sc Ire1-KR, in agreement with our previous reports (Guydosh et al., 2017; Kimmig et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) cleaved the BIP1 motif efficiently with the additional tolerance of any nucleotide at position −2.
source: By contrast, Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) cleaved the motif efficiently with the additional tolerance of any nucleotide at position −2, thus reducing the required sequence motif to only G and C nucleotides flanking the cleavage site (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Sp Ire1-KR and Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) are tolerant to loop size variation.
source: In further support of the notion that Sp Ire1-KR and Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) are tolerant to loop size variation, two of our stem-loop RNA substrates harboring mutations, U-5 → A and U+4 → A, respectively, which are predicted to contract the 9-membered loop to a 7-membered one, were efficiently cleaved by both enzymes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Sp Ire1-KR and Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) are promiscuous enzymes that recognize short RNA sequence motifs and can accept a range of loop sizes.
source: Together, these data affirm the notion that Sp Ire1-KR and Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) are promiscuous enzymes that recognize short RNA sequence motifs and can accept a range of loop sizes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Active Sc Ire1 oligomers are composed of multiple Ire1 back-to-back dimers that stack in a helical arrangement.
source: Active Sc Ire1 oligomers are composed of multiple Ire1 back-to-back dimers that stack in a helical arrangement (Korennykh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The convergent structure model of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) predicts a structural rearrangement at Ire1's dimer interface.
source: The convergent structure model of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) predicts a structural rearrangement at Ire1's dimer interface.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: In the WT Sc Ire1-KR dimer residues E988 and K992 of both protomers form a symmetric pair of salt bridges across the dimer interface.
source: Specifically, whereas in the WT Sc Ire1-KR dimer residues E988 and K992 of both protomers form a symmetric pair of salt bridges across the dimer interface (Figure 5B), these salt bridges are absent in the dimer of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) due to the charge reversal introduced by the K992D mutation.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: These salt bridges are absent in the dimer of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) due to the charge reversal introduced by the K992D mutation.
source: Specifically, whereas in the WT Sc Ire1-KR dimer residues E988 and K992 of both protomers form a symmetric pair of salt bridges across the dimer interface (Figure 5B), these salt bridges are absent in the dimer of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) due to the charge reversal introduced by the K992D mutation.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The model predicts the formation of a new pair of salt bridges in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R), connecting the two newly introduced amino acids D992 and R1059 across the protomer/protomer interface.
source: More interestingly, the model predicts the formation of a new pair of salt bridges in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R), connecting the two newly introduced amino acids D992 and R1059 across the protomer/protomer interface (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The MD simulation predicts these new bonds as stable features.
source: The MD simulation predicts these new bonds as stable features (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Molecular modeling suggests a structural rearrangement, resulting from the two interface mutations in Sc Ire1, which allows Sc Ire1 to assume the promiscuous 'pombe-like' state.
source: Thus, molecular modeling suggests a structural rearrangement, resulting from the two interface mutations in Sc Ire1, which, we propose, allows Sc Ire1 to assume the promiscuous 'pombe-like' state (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The predicted new salt bridges in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) are mediated by guanidinium-carboxylate bidentate interactions.
source: The predicted new salt bridges in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) are mediated by guanidinium-carboxylate bidentate interactions, which are among the strongest non-covalent interactions in proteins and are considerably stronger than the ammonium-carboxylate interaction seen in the salt bridges in WT Sc Ire1-KR (Masunov and Lazaridis, 2003).
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling and citation to previous work on interaction strengths.

claim: Guanidinium-carboxylate bidentate interactions are among the strongest non-covalent interactions in proteins and are considerably stronger than the ammonium-carboxylate interaction.
source: The predicted new salt bridges in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) are mediated by guanidinium-carboxylate bidentate interactions, which are among the strongest non-covalent interactions in proteins and are considerably stronger than the ammonium-carboxylate interaction seen in the salt bridges in WT Sc Ire1-KR (Masunov and Lazaridis, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The mutant enzyme should be more prone to form dimers/oligomers than WT Sc Ire1-KR.
source: Given that the interaction at the dimer interface is predicted to be stronger in mutant Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) than in WT Sc Ire1-KR, the mutant enzyme should be more prone to form dimers/oligomers than WT Sc Ire1-KR.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the molecular modeling results.

claim: WT Sc Ire1-KR was mostly monomeric, while Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) formed mostly dimers and tetramers.
source: Indeed, we confirmed this notion using protein crosslinking in vitro, followed by SDS-PAGE, showing that WT Sc Ire1-KR was mostly monomeric, while Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) formed mostly dimers and tetramers (Figure 5E, compare lanes 2 and 3 with lanes 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: For Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R), the dissociation constant (KD) is 0.98 μM, which is about 60-fold smaller than that of WT Sc Ire1-KR (KD = 57 μM).
source: For Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R), we calculated a dissociation constant (KD) of 0.98 μM, which is about 60-fold smaller than that of WT Sc Ire1-KR (KD = 57 μM).
evidence: This is supported by sedimentation equilibrium analytical ultracentrifugation data.

claim: The estimated gain in free energy of the predicted new salt bridges results in higher affinity within the back-to-back dimer, thus increasing the propensity of Ire1 to oligomerize.
source: Based on these results, we consider it likely that the estimated gain in free energy of the predicted new salt bridges results in higher affinity within the back-to-back dimer, thus increasing the propensity of Ire1 to oligomerize.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059A) did not form dimers.
source: Thus, as expected, Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059A) did not form dimers (Figure 5E, lanes 8 and 9) and displayed ~100 fold reduced cleavage efficiency on HAC1-derived and an additional 100-fold (i.e., overall ~10,000 fold) reduced cleavage rate on BIP1-derived RNA substrates (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059A) displayed ~100 fold reduced cleavage efficiency on HAC1-derived and an additional 100-fold (i.e., overall ~10,000 fold) reduced cleavage rate on BIP1-derived RNA substrates.
source: Thus, as expected, Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059A) did not form dimers (Figure 5E, lanes 8 and 9) and displayed ~100 fold reduced cleavage efficiency on HAC1-derived and an additional 100-fold (i.e., overall ~10,000 fold) reduced cleavage rate on BIP1-derived RNA substrates (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Breaking the pombe-like salt bridge arrangement restored Sc Ire1's ability to discriminate between substrate RNAs by ~100 fold.
source: Thus, surprisingly, breaking the pombe-like salt bridge arrangement restored Sc Ire1's ability to discriminate between substrate RNAs by ~100 fold (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Breaking the predicted salt bridges on Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) by mutating aspartate 992 to alanine abolished Ire1's RNase activity.
source: Breaking the predicted salt bridges on Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) by mutating aspartate 992 to alanine also abolished Ire1's RNase activity (Sc Ire1-KR(K992A,Y1059R); Figure 5—figure supplement 4), in this case reducing activity towards both HAC1- and BIP1-derived substrate RNAs beyond our detection limit (>10,000 fold).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(K992R,Y1059D) regained activity towards the BIP1-derived substrate.
source: We found that, while the overall cleavage rate remained 100-fold suppressed for both RNA substrates, Sc Ire1-KR(K992R,Y1059D) regained activity towards the BIP1-derived substrate (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 4) and formed dimers (Figure 5E, lanes 10 and 11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(K992R,Y1059D) formed dimers.
source: We found that, while the overall cleavage rate remained 100-fold suppressed for both RNA substrates, Sc Ire1-KR(K992R,Y1059D) regained activity towards the BIP1-derived substrate (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 4) and formed dimers (Figure 5E, lanes 10 and 11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: These experiments validate the predicted salt bridges on Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R).
source: Together, these experiments validate the predicted salt bridges on Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) and further underscore the notion that salt bridge rewiring to a pombe-like arrangement confers promiscuity to Ire1's RNase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Salt bridge rewiring to a pombe-like arrangement confers promiscuity to Ire1's RNase activity.
source: Together, these experiments validate the predicted salt bridges on Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) and further underscore the notion that salt bridge rewiring to a pombe-like arrangement confers promiscuity to Ire1's RNase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: 175 out of 230 of the Ire1 orthologs, including human Ire1α and Ire1β, have the S. pombe-like pattern.
source: We found that 175 out of 230 of the Ire1 orthologs, including human Ire1α and Ire1β, have the S. pombe-like pattern, characterized by significant amino acid variation at position 988, a negatively charged amino acid (aspartate or glutamate) at position 992, and a positively charged amino acid (lysine or arginine) at position 1059.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison of 230 Ire1 orthologs.

claim: The apparent co-evolution of position 992 and 1059 further supports the existence of an inter-molecular salt bridge.
source: The apparent co-evolution of position 992 and 1059 further supports the existence of an inter-molecular salt bridge.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sequence comparison data.

claim: Thirty-three out of 230 of the Ire1 orthologs have the S. cerevisiae-like pattern.
source: Thirty-three out of 230 of the Ire1 orthologs have the S. cerevisiae-like pattern—with a negatively charged amino acid (aspartate or glutamate) at position 988, a positively charged amino acid (lysine or arginine) at position 992 and, in most cases, a tyrosine at position 1059.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison of 230 Ire1 orthologs.

claim: Co-evolution of position 988 and 992 supports their interaction at the dimer interface.
source: Co-evolution of position 988 and 992 supports their interaction at the dimer interface.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sequence comparison data.

claim: The salt bridge between D992 and R1059' in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) reduced the distance between the two juxtaposed α-helices.
source: Specifically, the salt bridge between D992 and R1059' in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) reduced the distance between the two juxtaposed α-helices from which their sidechains protrude (α1-helix: aa 983–998; α4-helix: aa 1048–1064, as named in Lee et al., 2008; Figure 6C), while, concomitantly, the loss of the salt bridges between E988 and K992 present in WT Sc Ire1-KR allows an increase in the distance between α1-helices from which both of these amino acid side chains protrude (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The loss of the salt bridges between E988 and K992 present in WT Sc Ire1-KR allows an increase in the distance between α1-helices.
source: Specifically, the salt bridge between D992 and R1059' in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) reduced the distance between the two juxtaposed α-helices from which their sidechains protrude (α1-helix: aa 983–998; α4-helix: aa 1048–1064, as named in Lee et al., 2008; Figure 6C), while, concomitantly, the loss of the salt bridges between E988 and K992 present in WT Sc Ire1-KR allows an increase in the distance between α1-helices from which both of these amino acid side chains protrude (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The distance between the centers of mass of the two α1-helices was increased by about 3 Å in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) compared to WT Sc Ire1-KR.
source: First, we measured the distance between the centers of mass of the two α1-helices throughout the 20 ns simulation trajectories, which was increased by about 3 Å in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) compared to WT Sc Ire1-KR.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The distance between the α carbons of R1039 and H1061' was decreased by about 5 Å in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) compared to WT Sc Ire1-KR.
source: Second, we measured the distance between the α carbons of R1039 involved in RNA substrate binding and H1061' involved in phosphodiester bond hydrolysis (Korennykh et al., 2011), which was decreased by about 5 Å in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) compared to WT Sc Ire1-KR (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: The mutations that increase Ire1's RNase promiscuity are predicted to change both the RNase-RNase interface and the relative alignment of important elements in the catalytic site of the Ire1 dimer.
source: Therefore, the mutations that increase Ire1's RNase promiscuity are predicted to change both the RNase-RNase interface and the relative alignment of important elements in the catalytic site of the Ire1 dimer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: RNase L mediates the antiviral and apoptotic effects of interferons in mammalian cells.
source: The kinase/RNase domain of Ire1 is homologous to the kinase homology (KH) and kinase extension nuclease (KEN) domains of the Ribonuclease L (RNase L), which mediates the antiviral and apoptotic effects of interferons in mammalian cells (Chakrabarti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Upon activation, RNase L forms homodimers.
source: Upon activation, RNase L forms homodimers (Han et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2014) and cleaves mRNAs with a sequence motif of UN|N, where N can be any ribonucleotide (Han et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RNase L cleaves mRNAs with a sequence motif of UN|N, where N can be any ribonucleotide.
source: Upon activation, RNase L forms homodimers (Han et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2014) and cleaves mRNAs with a sequence motif of UN|N, where N can be any ribonucleotide (Han et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: At the RNase-RNase dimer interface of RNase L, N601' and E671 form a pair of intermolecular hydrogen bonds between RNase L's α1- and α4-helix.
source: At the RNase-RNase dimer interface of RNase L, N601' and E671 form a pair of intermolecular hydrogen bonds between RNase L's α1- and α4-helix (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Han et al., 2014) (in RNase L the α1-helix spans aa W589-V599 and the α4-helix aa V659-H672, as defined in Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and citation to previous work.

claim: RNase L and Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) share a conserved arrangement by which their α1- and α4-helix are connected.
source: Thus, RNase L and Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) share a conserved arrangement by which their α1- and α4-helix are connected.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from structural comparison.

claim: The protomer alignment of RNase L closely resembles that of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R).
source: In further support of this notion, we analyzed RNase L using the metrics defined in Figure 6E and found that the protomer alignment of RNase L closely resembles that of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A & B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6E and supplementary figures.

claim: RNase L and Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R), both of which have promiscuous RNase activity, share a similar protomer alignment.
source: Thus, RNase L and Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R), both of which have promiscuous RNase activity, share a similar protomer alignment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claim: Ire1 from S. cerevisiae is highly specific, precisely cleaving but a single mRNA in the cell (HAC1 mRNA) at its two splice junctions to excise the intron and initiate mRNA splicing.
source: At one extreme lies Ire1 from S. cerevisiae, which is highly specific, precisely cleaving but a single mRNA in the cell (HAC1 mRNA) at its two splice junctions to excise the intron and initiate mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Ire1 from S. pombe is highly promiscuous cleaving numerous mRNAs at recognition sites that share but a three-nucleotide consensus in a variably sized loop.
source: At the other extreme lies Ire1 from S. pombe, which is highly promiscuous cleaving numerous mRNAs at recognition sites that share but a three-nucleotide consensus in a variably sized loop.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Ire1's cytosolic kinase/RNase domains determine whether Ire1 works in the specific S. cerevisiae-like or relatively non-specific S. pombe-like modality.
source: We previously showed by domain swapping experiments that Ire1's cytosolic kinase/RNase domains determine whether Ire1 works in the specific S. cerevisiae-like or relatively non-specific S. pombe-like modality.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The S. cerevisiae Ire1's RNase specificity becomes promiscuous when only two amino acids, K992 and Y1059, are replaced by aspartate and arginine respectively.
source: Using a growth assay based on heterologous expression of Ire1 kinase/RNase domains in bacteria that reports on Ire1's RNase promiscuity, we found that the S. cerevisiae Ire1's RNase specificity becomes promiscuous when only two amino acids, K992 and Y1059, are replaced by aspartate and arginine respectively, which are the corresponding amino acids in S. pombe Ire1.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) retained activity towards HAC1 mRNA-derived stem-loops, which is inert to cleavage by Sp Ire1.
source: While these replacements rendered Sc Ire1 more promiscuous, they did not entirely switch Sc Ire1's substrate RNA profile to that of Sp Ire1: Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) retained activity towards HAC1 mRNA-derived stem-loops, which is inert to cleavage by Sp Ire1 (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: The K992D and Y1059R mutations rendered Sc Ire1 even more promiscuous than Sp Ire1.
source: The K992D and Y1059R mutations therefore rendered Sc Ire1 even more promiscuous than Sp Ire1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The identified residues cause rewiring of two symmetry-related inter-molecular salt-bridges at Ire1's RNase-RNase interface within the back-to-back dimer.
source: MD simulations and biochemical assays revealed that the identified residues cause rewiring of two symmetry-related inter-molecular salt-bridges at Ire1's RNase-RNase interface within the back-to-back dimer.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulations and biochemical assays.

claim: The vast majority of species is predicted to have RIDD-enabled Ire1s as indicated by their S. pombe-like salt bridge pattern.
source: By this criterion, the vast majority of species is predicted to have RIDD-enabled Ire1s as indicated by their S. pombe-like salt bridge pattern.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sequence comparison data.

claim: Both human Ire1α and Ire1β have a S. pombe-like interface pattern.
source: Even though human Ire1α and Ire1β have different RNase specificity (Imagawa et al., 2008), both have a S. pombe-like interface pattern.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and citation to previous work.

claim: Both human Ire1 isoforms are able to perform RIDD.
source: This characteristic is consistent with both human Ire1 isoforms being able to perform RIDD (Hollien et al., 2009; Iwawaki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The ability of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) to conduct both HAC1-specific and promiscuous cleavage resembles that of human Ire1α in its fully phosphorylated, oligomeric state.
source: Of note, the ability of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) to conduct both HAC1-specific and promiscuous cleavage resembles that of human Ire1α in its fully phosphorylated, oligomeric state, while the more restricted activity of Sc Ire1 resembles that of dimeric human Ire1α (Le Thomas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The more restricted activity of Sc Ire1 resembles that of dimeric human Ire1α.
source: Of note, the ability of Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) to conduct both HAC1-specific and promiscuous cleavage resembles that of human Ire1α in its fully phosphorylated, oligomeric state, while the more restricted activity of Sc Ire1 resembles that of dimeric human Ire1α (Le Thomas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The RNase-RNase interface is a determinant for Ire1's RNase specificity.
source: Surprisingly, our work identified the RNase-RNase interface, rather than regions involved in substrate binding or catalysis, as a determinant for Ire1's RNase specificity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Conserved salt bridges determine the relative protomer alignment.
source: We show evidence that conserved salt bridges determine the relative protomer alignment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and molecular modeling.

claim: In the composite RNase active site of the back-to-back dimer, the relative distance of residues that contribute to cleavage from both protomers is changed.
source: In the composite RNase active site of the back-to-back dimer, the relative distance of residues that contribute to cleavage from both protomers is changed (Korennykh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by molecular modeling and citation to previous work.

claim: The small molecule, quercetin, stabilizes S. cerevisiae Ire1's dimers/oligomers and increase its RNase activity.
source: The small molecule, quercetin, which stabilizes S. cerevisiae Ire1's dimers/oligomers and increase its RNase activity (Wiseman et al., 2010), binds to the same site where the two mutations identified in this study are located.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Quercetin binds to the same site where the two mutations identified in this study are located.
source: The small molecule, quercetin, which stabilizes S. cerevisiae Ire1's dimers/oligomers and increase its RNase activity (Wiseman et al., 2010), binds to the same site where the two mutations identified in this study are located.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Quercetin binding does not change Ire1 protomer alignment and hence is not expected to alter Ire1's RNase specificity.
source: However, quercetin binding does not change Ire1 protomer alignment and hence is not expected to alter Ire1's RNase specificity (Wiseman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Modulation of the RNase selectivity by targeting the quercetin pocket is conceivable.
source: Nevertheless, modulation of the RNase selectivity by targeting the quercetin pocket is conceivable.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: In human Ire1, crystal structures showed that the two RNase domains in the dimer are further apart in the inactive state than in the active state.
source: In human Ire1, crystal structures showed that the two RNase domains in the dimer are further apart in the inactive state than in the active state (Joshi et al., 2015), and our data similarly indicate that breaking the salt bridges in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) by either changing the aspartate or the arginine to alanine leads to profound reduction of activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Breaking the salt bridges in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) by either changing the aspartate or the arginine to alanine leads to profound reduction of activity.
source: In human Ire1, crystal structures showed that the two RNase domains in the dimer are further apart in the inactive state than in the active state (Joshi et al., 2015), and our data similarly indicate that breaking the salt bridges in Sc Ire1-KR(K992D,Y1059R) by either changing the aspartate or the arginine to alanine leads to profound reduction of activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The more promiscuous RIDD modality of human Ire1α requires phosphorylation-driven oligomerization.
source: Related work demonstrates that the more promiscuous RIDD modality of human Ire1α requires phosphorylation-driven oligomerization, which can be prevented by an oligomer-disrupting mutation at the RNase-RNase interface within the back-to-back dimers (Le Thomas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation-driven oligomerization of human Ire1α can be prevented by an oligomer-disrupting mutation at the RNase-RNase interface within the back-to-back dimers.
source: Related work demonstrates that the more promiscuous RIDD modality of human Ire1α requires phosphorylation-driven oligomerization, which can be prevented by an oligomer-disrupting mutation at the RNase-RNase interface within the back-to-back dimers (Le Thomas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Ire1 RNase domain's dimer interface is a dynamic site through which both activity and substrate specificity can be regulated.
source: Thus together, the data presented here demonstrate that Ire1 RNase domain's dimer interface is a dynamic site through which both activity and substrate specificity can be regulated.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
